Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- A suburban Philadelphia swim club has invited children from a largely minority day-care center to come back after a June reversal that fueled allegations of racism against the club, a spokeswoman said Sunday. Some kids from the Creative Steps Day Care center say club members made racial remarks. The development came during a hastily called Sunday afternoon meeting of the Valley Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania. Club members voted overwhelmingly to try to work things out with the day-care center, which accused some swim club members of making racist comments to black and Hispanic children contracted to use the pool, said Bernice Duesler, the club director's wife. Duesler said the club canceled its contract with the Creative Steps day-care because of safety, crowding and noise concerns, not racism. "As long as we can work out safety issues, we'd like to have them back," she told CNN. She said the club has been subpoenaed by the state Human Rights Commission, which has begun a fact-finding investigation, "and the legal advice was to try to get together with these camps, " Duesler added. Alethea Wright, Creative Steps' director, said, "They should have done that before." Wright has repeatedly lambasted the club for its tepid response to the charges and said the children in her care were "emotionally damaged" by the incident. "These children are scarred. How can I take those children back there?" she said. However, Wright's lawyer, Carolyn Nicholas, said the center will give the Valley Club's offer "due consideration" once it is received and looks forward to sitting down with the parties. "The children are our primary concern," Nicholas told CNN. Swimming privileges for about 65 children from Creative Steps were revoked after their first visit June 29. Some children said white members of the club made racist comments to the children, asking why "black children were there" and raising concerns that "they might steal from us." Days later, the day-care center's $1,950 check was returned, Wright said. Club director John Duesler told CNN that he had underestimated the amount of children who would participate, and the club was unable to supervise that many kids. He called his club "very diverse," and said it had offered to let day camps in the Philadelphia area use his facility after budget cuts forced some pools in the area to close. Wright has rejected the camp's contention that the swim club's pool was overcrowded. The club had accepted a 10-to-1 ratio of children to adults and was considering adding up to three lifeguards, according to e-mails obtained by CNN. But John Duesler said last week that the Valley Club also canceled contracts with two other day-care centers because of safety and overcrowding issues. The Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission launched an investigation last week after allegations of racism at the Valley Club. The commission said that as part of any investigation, the two sides eventually could be asked to sit down face-to-face with its investigators. "We always encourage opposing parties to communicate with one another if they feel they can resolve these issues amicably," Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman said. Bernice Duesler said she wasn't yet sure how the club will "reach out" to Creative Steps and the other two camps. And Wright said she still has concerns about the issue. "Are the members who made those comments still there?" she asked.

The Valley Club, located in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania, held an emergency meeting Sunday afternoon. Members voted by a wide margin to seek a resolution with Creative Steps Day Care, according to Bernice Duesler, the wife of the club’s director.

Creative Steps had arranged for its children to use the pool, but the agreement was terminated after their first visit. Several Black and Hispanic children said white club members questioned why Black children were present and expressed fears that the children might steal from them.

She also said the Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission had subpoenaed the club as part of a fact-finding inquiry. According to Duesler, legal counsel recommended that the club attempt to meet with the day-care programs involved.

Creative Steps director Alethea Wright responded that the club should have taken that step earlier. Wright has repeatedly criticized what she considers the club’s inadequate reaction to the allegations and said the experience caused emotional harm to the children.

She questioned how she could bring the children back to a place where they had been left scarred by the incident.

However, Carolyn Nicholas, Wright’s attorney, said Creative Steps would carefully review the Valley Club’s proposal after receiving it. She added that the center was prepared to meet with the other parties and emphasized to CNN that the children’s welfare remained the central concern.

Approximately 65 Creative Steps children lost access to the pool following their initial visit on June 29. Wright said the day-care center’s payment of $1,950 was refunded several days later.

Valley Club director John Duesler previously told CNN that he had miscalculated how many children would attend and that the club did not have enough supervision for such a large group. He described the membership as highly diverse. He also said the club had invited Philadelphia-area day camps to use the facility after budget reductions led to the closure of some local pools.

Wright disputed the club’s claim that overcrowding was the problem. E-mails obtained by CNN showed that the Valley Club had approved a ratio of 10 children for every adult and had been considering hiring as many as three additional lifeguards.

John Duesler said last week that the club had also ended agreements with two other day-care centers, likewise citing crowding and safety concerns.

The Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission opened an investigation the previous week in response to the racism allegations. The commission said its inquiry could eventually include an in-person meeting between the two sides and investigators.

Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman said the agency routinely urges opposing parties to speak directly when they believe an amicable settlement may be possible.

Bernice Duesler said the Valley Club had not yet determined how it would contact Creative Steps or the other two programs.

Wright, meanwhile, said she continued to have reservations, including whether the club members accused of making the remarks were still present.

### Philadelphia-area swim club invites minority children back amid discrimination allegations

**HUNTINGDON VALLEY, Pennsylvania** — A suburban Philadelphia swim club has invited a group of mostly Black and Hispanic children to return after the cancellation of their summer swimming arrangement prompted allegations of racial discrimination.

The children, who attended the Creative Steps day camp, had visited the Valley Swim Club in Huntingdon Valley under an agreement allowing them to use the pool. Camp officials said the children heard racially charged remarks from some club members and were later told the arrangement had been canceled.

The club denied that race played a role, saying the decision was based on concerns about crowding, safety and the pool’s capacity to accommodate a large group. Club officials refunded the camp’s payment but later reversed course and invited the children back.

“We deeply regret that this situation has been interpreted as racially motivated,” the club said in a statement, adding that it wanted to resolve the dispute and welcome the campers again.

Creative Steps officials said the episode left many of the children feeling rejected and humiliated. Parents called for an investigation and questioned whether the invitation could repair the harm.

Pennsylvania civil rights authorities began reviewing the allegations. The dispute also drew national attention, with advocacy groups urging the club to address both the cancellation and the reported comments made during the children’s visit.

It was not immediately clear whether the camp would accept the invitation to return.

In 2009, the Valley Swim Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania, became the center of a racial-discrimination controversy after it canceled a swimming arrangement with Creative Steps, a Philadelphia day-care center serving mostly Black and Hispanic children.

Creative Steps had paid the club about $1,950 for roughly 60–65 campers to swim there weekly. After their first visit, staff and children said club members made racist remarks, including asking why “all these Black kids” were there and suggesting the children might affect the pool. Day-care director Alethea Wright said the children felt humiliated and unwelcome.

The club refunded the payment and canceled the arrangement. Club president John Duesler initially said members were concerned the children would change the club’s “complexion” and “atmosphere.” He later apologized for that wording and denied racial bias, saying the club had simply underestimated crowding, staffing, safety and pool-capacity problems. The club also noted that it canceled agreements with other day-care groups.

The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission investigated after discrimination complaints were filed. It ultimately found probable cause that the club had discriminated on the basis of race, citing the children’s treatment, members’ comments and evidence that white swimmers were treated differently. The controversy led to broader legal action, including a U.S. Justice Department case. The club later filed for bankruptcy and closed, and a 2012 settlement provided approximately $1.1 million for the affected children, their families and Creative Steps.

# Pennsylvania Swim Club Reconsiders Ban on Black and Hispanic Children After Racism Allegations

**HUNTINGDON VALLEY, Pa.** — A suburban Philadelphia swim club said it would reconsider its decision to revoke swimming privileges for a day-care group of 65 mostly Black and Hispanic children after parents and camp officials alleged that club members made racist remarks during the children’s first visit.

The Valley Swim Club, a private club in Huntingdon Valley, had entered into an agreement allowing children from Creative Steps, a Philadelphia day-care and summer program, to use its pool on Mondays during the summer. The arrangement was canceled after the group’s first visit in late June 2009, and the club refunded the program’s payment.

Creative Steps director Alethea Wright said several children reported hearing club members question why Black children were at the pool. One widely reported remark was, “What are all these Black kids doing here?” Parents said the children felt humiliated and confused by the encounter.

Club officials initially denied that race motivated the cancellation. They said the number of children was larger and more disruptive than expected and raised concerns about crowding and safety.

However, comments attributed to club president John Duesler intensified criticism. Duesler told reporters that some members were concerned the children would “change the complexion” and “the atmosphere” of the club. He later said the word “complexion” had been used to refer to the club’s environment rather than the children’s race, but the phrasing drew widespread condemnation.

As the dispute gained national attention, the club’s board said it would review the cancellation and consider reinstating the agreement with Creative Steps. Club representatives expressed regret over the way the situation had been handled and said they did not condone racial discrimination.

The children’s parents and civil-rights advocates said the sequence of events — the alleged comments, the cancellation immediately after the first visit and the refund — raised serious questions about whether the group had been excluded because of race.

Wright said the children had been excited about the chance to swim but returned from the visit asking why other people did not want them at the pool. For families, she said, the dispute was not simply about access to a recreational facility but about the emotional effect on children who believed they had been rejected because of their skin color.

The incident also prompted scrutiny from the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission, which enforces the state’s anti-discrimination laws. Although the Valley Swim Club described itself as a private organization, officials examined whether its contracts with outside groups and other operating practices placed it under public-accommodation provisions.

Civil-rights organizations called for a formal investigation and said reconsidering the decision would not, by itself, resolve the allegations. They urged the club to establish clear nondiscrimination policies, train staff and address the conduct of any members who made offensive comments.

The controversy quickly spread beyond Pennsylvania. News reports and online discussions drew comparisons to earlier eras when Black Americans were excluded from swimming pools and other recreational facilities. Supporters of the Creative Steps children offered alternative swimming opportunities and assistance to the program.

For the Valley Swim Club, the decision to revisit the cancellation marked a reversal from its initial defense of the action. But parents said any offer to return would have to include assurances that the children would be welcomed and protected from further mistreatment.

The club’s board was expected to discuss whether to restore the group’s swimming privileges and how to respond to the broader allegations. Meanwhile, state officials continued gathering information about the agreement, the cancellation and what occurred during the children’s visit.

The case became a national flashpoint because of the stark disagreement at its center: club officials portrayed the cancellation as a matter of capacity and safety, while Creative Steps families said the children were made to feel unwelcome before being excluded from the pool.

Whatever the board’s final decision, advocates said the episode demonstrated that reversing the ban was only the first step. The larger question, they said, was whether the club would acknowledge the harm experienced by the children and take concrete action to ensure that race played no role in future membership or access decisions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

### Valley Swim Club controversy

In July 2009, the Valley Swim Club in Huntingdon Valley, outside Philadelphia, came under scrutiny after canceling an arrangement with **Creative Steps**, a Northeast Philadelphia day-care center whose campers were predominantly Black and Hispanic.

Creative Steps had paid about **$1,950** for roughly 60 children to swim at the private club once a week. After their first visit, the club refunded the payment and ended the agreement. Club officials cited overcrowding, inadequate staffing and safety concerns, saying several day-care groups had brought more children than expected.

Parents and staff alleged racial discrimination. Some children said they heard club members make racist comments. The controversy intensified when club president **John Duesler** said the children had changed the “complexion” and “atmosphere” of the club. He later apologized for the wording and maintained that the cancellation was based on safety and capacity, not race.

Amid national criticism and an inquiry by the **Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission**, the club’s board voted to reinstate Creative Steps’ contract and invited the children to return. Day-care director **Alethea Wright** declined the immediate offer, saying the children no longer felt welcome or safe and that the club had not adequately addressed what happened.

The state commission later found probable cause that racial discrimination had occurred. The financially troubled swim club subsequently filed for bankruptcy and closed.

**Day-care center alleges racial discrimination after swim club cancels agreement**

**PHILADELPHIA (CNN) —** A suburban Philadelphia swim club denied allegations of racial discrimination after canceling an arrangement that allowed children from a predominantly Black and Hispanic day-care center to use its pool.

Creative Steps Inc. paid the Valley Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania, about $1,950 for its children to swim there during the summer. But after the group’s first visit in June 2009, the club ended the agreement and returned the money.

Creative Steps director Alethea Wright said some children heard club members making comments about their race.

“These children are scarred,” Wright said. She said one child asked her, “Why didn’t they want us there?”

Wright also said she was told the children would “change the complexion” of the club.

Valley Club representatives said the decision was based on crowding and safety, not race. In a written statement, the club called the allegations of racism “completely untrue” and said officials realized after the first visit that the pool could not safely accommodate the additional swimmers.

Club president John Duesler initially told a Philadelphia television station, “There was concern that a lot of kids would change the complexion … and the atmosphere of the club.” He later said the remark had been misunderstood and that he was referring to the character and capacity of the swimming environment, not the children’s race.

The club said it had also canceled or reconsidered arrangements involving other groups because of pool capacity. Officials maintained that no child had been barred individually and that the day-care center’s payment was refunded.

Brian Mildenberg, an attorney representing Creative Steps, rejected the club’s explanation.

“The pool took the money and entered into a contract with these children,” Mildenberg said. “Then, after they saw the children, they changed their minds.”

The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission opened an investigation into whether the club had violated state anti-discrimination law. Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman described the allegations as serious but emphasized that the agency would determine the facts through its investigative process.

“If proven, these allegations would constitute illegal discrimination,” Glassman said.

The dispute drew national attention and prompted several organizations and individuals to offer the children access to other swimming facilities. Valley Club officials, meanwhile, said they regretted the hurt caused by the cancellation but continued to deny that race played any role in their decision.
